title: 3  Greatest Common Divisor and Least Common Multiple
text:
3.2 Example
Let’s take two integers, say 24 and 36:

The factors of 24 are: 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 8, 12, 24.
The factors of 36 are: 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 9, 12, 18, 36.
The common factors are: 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 12.

Out of these, the greatest one is 12. So, the GCD of 24 and 36 is 12.
crumbs: 3  Greatest Common Divisor and Least Common Multiple

title: 3  Greatest Common Divisor and Least Common Multiple
text:
3.3 Euclidean Algorithm
The Euclidean algorithm is a well-known method for finding the GCD of two numbers. It is based on the principle that the GCD of two numbers also divides their difference. Here’s how it works:

Given two numbers a and b, replace a with b and b with the remainder of the division of a by b (a % b).
Repeat this process until b becomes 0.
The GCD is the non-zero number remaining.
crumbs: 3  Greatest Common Divisor and Least Common Multiple

title: 3  Greatest Common Divisor and Least Common Multiple
text:
3.4 Steps in the Euclidean Algorithm
For example, let’s find the GCD of 48 and 18 using the Euclidean algorithm:

Initial values: a = 48, b = 18.
Compute 48 % 18, which is 12. Update a to 18 and b to 12.
Compute 18 % 12, which is 6. Update a to 12 and b to 6.
Compute 12 % 6, which is 0. Update a to 6 and b to 0.
Now, b is 0, so the GCD is the current value of a, which is 6.

In summary, the GCD of two integers is the largest integer that divides both of them without leaving a remainder, and it can be efficiently computed using the Euclidean algorithm.

title: 13  Topological Sort
text:
13.1 The Algorithm
Topological sorting is a linear ordering of vertices in a directed acyclic graph (DAG) such that for every directed edge uv from vertex u to vertex v, vertex u comes before v in the ordering. Topological sorting is only possible if the graph has no directed cycles, i.e., it must be a DAG.
Topological sorting is commonly used in:
One common method to perform topological sorting is Kahn’s Algorithm, which uses in-degree (the number of incoming edges) of vertices:

title: 13  Topological Sort
text:
Scheduling tasks: Determining the order in which tasks should be performed, where some tasks must be done before others.
Build systems: Resolving dependencies in build systems, where some components must be built before others.
Course prerequisite ordering: Determining the order in which courses should be taken based on prerequisites.



Initialize:

Calculate in-degrees of all vertices.
Initialize a queue and enqueue all vertices with in-degree 0.

Process the queue:

While the queue is not empty:

Dequeue a vertex u and add it to the topological order.
For each adjacent vertex v (i.e., vertices where there is an edge u -> v):

Decrease the in-degree of v by 1.
If in-degree of v becomes 0, enqueue v.



Check for cycles:

If the topological order contains all vertices, the graph is a DAG.
If not, the graph contains a cycle, and topological sorting is not possible.

title: 130. Surrounded Regions
text:
Problem
The original problem is defined here: 130. Surrounded Regions.
There are two types of cells in the board: X cells and O cells. O cells can be connected to each other if they are adjacent horizontally or vertically. Some connected O cells are surrounded by X cells if none of them are located on the borders of the board. The key is to identify all the surrounded O cells and mark them as X.
